hints: Think about the two parts every single virus must have to work, its genetic instructions inside and its protective coat outside. What polymers are those made from?
Now ask if every prokaryote and every virus must have polysaccharides. Do all viruses have a sugary envelope or capsule, and do all prokaryotes (remember Mycoplasma with no wall) have them?
walkthrough:
**Start with viruses - what is always there?**

All viruses contain nucleic acid to carry their genes, so that is polynucleotide (DNA or RNA). All viruses also have a protein capsid around it, so that is polypeptide. Lovely, that gives us 1 and 2 for viruses.

**Check prokaryotes - what is always there?**

All prokaryotic cells contain DNA and RNA for genes and protein synthesis, so polynucleotides are always present. They also contain many proteins and enzymes made of polypeptides, for example in membranes, cytoplasm and ribosomes. So 1 and 2 are present in all prokaryotes too.

**Test polysaccharides carefully**

Polysaccharides are found in many places, like bacterial cell walls and capsules, and in the envelopes of some viruses. But the key word is all. Not all viruses have a glycoprotein envelope, and not all prokaryotes have a wall or capsule. So 3 is not universal, leaving 1 and 2 only.

options.A: Incorrect because it includes 3. Polysaccharides are common but not present in all viruses and all prokaryotes.
options.B: Correct because polynucleotides (viral nucleic acid, bacterial DNA and RNA) and polypeptides (viral capsid, cellular proteins and enzymes) are found in every virus and every prokaryote.
options.C: Incorrect because it includes polysaccharides but misses polypeptides, yet every virus has a protein capsid and every prokaryote has proteins.
options.D: Incorrect because it misses polynucleotides, yet every virus has DNA or RNA and every prokaryote has DNA and RNA.
